```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Brief A shows a market with paid tiers at every level: $29-99/mo (NeverFined), $49/mo or $490/yr (ExpirationOps), $500-800/location/yr (ClearBot), and $3,999+/yr enterprise (Mosey). Harbor's License Manager has 212 Google reviews. Brief B's comparables cluster at $0-29/mo, and at least three competitors (Nalvis engine, BreakShield beta, mendapi CLI, Ripple) are free or open source. That directly undercuts B's $20-50/mo price hypothesis, as B's own open questions concede.",
    "A's buyers are finance and ops leads with an ops/compliance budget who are unlikely to self-build. B's buyers are engineers who can adopt free OSS alternatives or build their own, which makes a first sale within 90 days harder.",
    "B carries trust and liability risks a solo operator cannot easily clear. Customers must grant PR-opening access to their source code. mendapi's cited studies show raw spec-diff over-reporting by about 8x. Fintech and payment-API buyers, the highest payers, demand security reviews. A's main liability is handled with a one-time attorney consult and a 'tracking only, not advice' posture that competitors already use.",
    "Both briefs describe crowded markets with no clear wedge, so neither wins on differentiation. A comes out ahead because its market shows more evidence that customers pay, and a thin, manually maintained tracker plausibly matches the low-end paid comparables."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Brief B's CAC benchmark ($248 median devtools CAC, 9.4-month payback) comes from a source that B itself flags as containing a prompt-injection attempt and 'directional only'. It is the only quantitative support for B's main low-cost channel, so it should count as effectively missing. B's demand quotes also show pain from breaking changes but no willingness to pay. Its price anchor rests on a $29/mo competitor list price, with no evidence that anyone actually pays it while free alternatives exist.",
  "confidence_note": "Low-to-moderate confidence. Both ideas face seven or six live competitors and lack a defined wedge. A's demand evidence is thin and partly mismatched: three Reddit posts, two of them about individual professional licensure (engineer, therapist) rather than small multi-state businesses' operating licenses. A's own case against notes that a six-week build likely ships a subset of what buyers already get for $29-49/mo. The decision rests mainly on A showing stronger proof that its market pays rather than on any advantage in demand evidence."
}
```
